detail:
The Ehlers-Danlos Society defines hypermobility spectrum disorders as a group of conditions related to joint hypermobility, diagnosed after other possible answers are excluded, including any of the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes such as hypermobile EDS (hEDS). The essential difference between HSD and hEDS lies in the stricter criteria for hEDS; the Society states plainly that HSD, just like hEDS, can have significant effects, and the two can be equal in severity.

The Society describes a spectrum running from asymptomatic joint hypermobility through HSD to hEDS, with HSD subtypes based on which joints are involved (generalized, peripheral, localized, or historical). Beyond loose joints themselves, HSD involves secondary musculoskeletal manifestations: macrotrauma such as dislocations and subluxations, microtrauma, and chronic pain, along with problems like fatigue, headaches, gastrointestinal issues, and autonomic dysfunction that are often seen as part of HSD. This app's library also files its hEDS management entries under HSD, because the Society describes the management principles as the same for both.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about evaluation for symptomatic joint hypermobility.
sourceVideoTitle: What are the hypermobility spectrum disorders? (The Ehlers-Danlos Society)
summary: The Ehlers-Danlos Society describes hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) as connective tissue disorders in which joint hypermobility causes real symptoms such as pain, instability, and injury, but the stricter criteria for hypermobile EDS are not met.
takeaways: hsd and heds can be equal in severity
the difference is the stricter heds checklist, not how much it hurts
diagnosis comes after other conditions are excluded
management follows the same principles as heds; ask your doctor
title: Hypermobility spectrum disorders: symptomatic loose joints
